title: Image weight on a photography-heavy page
excerpt: Crop each photograph to its slot, send a modern format, and write alt text that matches the frame. A beautiful picture can still be the wrong number of bytes.
alt: Smooth overlapping waves of blue, violet, and warm orange. The broad color fields fit a piece about sending a photograph at the size the page actually uses.
caption: The frame and the file size are both decisions. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How should photographs be prepared for a web page?
faqs.answer: Crop them to the slot they will fill, including a separate crop when the phone layout uses a different ratio. Export a modern format such as AVIF or WebP at a quality you have looked at, in several widths, and tell the browser which width the layout needs. Set width and height so the text does not jump when the file arrives.

faqs.question: What is a good target for the main photograph?
faqs.answer: Google's Core Web Vitals guidance asks for largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds and cumulative layout shift under 0.1. On a photography-heavy page the main picture is often the largest element, so its bytes and its reserved box are the practical levers. Do not lazy-load that first image. Do lazy-load pictures below the fold.

faqs.question: What should image alt text say?
faqs.answer: What is actually in the frame: the subject, the setting, and any detail the page is relying on, such as a product color. Leave the alt empty only when the image is decorative and the sentence nearby already carries the point. Do not stuff a keyword into the alt. If the crop changes, rewrite the alt to match the crop.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
To optimize images for websites, crop to the slot, send a modern format, and write alt text that matches the frame. A beautiful photograph can still be the wrong number of bytes. The picture and the file are different decisions. The art direction picks the frame. The delivery makes that frame arrive without shoving the rest of the page aside.

Do both. A light file of the wrong crop is still the wrong picture. A perfect crop at several megabytes is still a slow page.

## Crop to the slot you actually have

Design the slot first. A hero at a known ratio, a portrait in a column, a full-bleed band. Then crop the photograph to that ratio, with the subject inside the safe area. Do not upload the original and hope the browser's cover-fit will be kind. Cover-fit will cut off heads, signs, and the edge of a product at exactly the sizes you did not check.

Export the crop you mean. If the mobile slot is a different ratio, art-direct a second crop rather than shrinking the desktop frame until the subject is a speck. Two crops, chosen, are lighter than one enormous file that tries to serve both and serves neither well.

Set the width and height in the page so the browser reserves the box before the file arrives. Google's [Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) treat cumulative layout shift as a core measure, and a good experience stays under 0.1. An image that loads and pushes the headline down is that metric, in the most visible place on the page. The reserved box also stops the reader from clicking the wrong thing while the photograph arrives.

Largest contentful paint has a target of 2.5 seconds in the same guidance. On a photography-heavy page, the photograph is often the largest element, so it is what that clock is timing. Cropping to the slot is the first reduction in bytes. A 4000-pixel-wide file in an 800-pixel column spends the reader's data on pixels you will throw away.

## A modern format, and a size for the screen

Serve a format the current web can decode efficiently, such as AVIF or WebP, with a fallback your template already knows how to negotiate. The point is a smaller file at a quality you have looked at, not a format badge. Export, look at the edges of type in the photograph and at skin and sky, and reject a file that smears. Then look at the byte size. If it is still heavy, the crop is too large or the quality setting is nostalgic for print.

Generate a few widths and let the browser choose, using `srcset` and `sizes` that match the slot. `sizes` is the part people skip, and it is the part that tells the browser how wide the image will be on the screen. A wrong `sizes` will download the huge file on a phone. Write it from the layout: full viewport in the hero, a third of the viewport in a three-column grid, and so on. Check the downloaded size in the network panel on a narrow window and a wide one.

Do not lazy-load the image that is the largest element in the first view. Load it early. Lazy-load the photographs below the fold, where the person has not arrived yet. Lazy-loading the hero is a way to make the metric worse while feeling modern.

A tiny placeholder in the right ratio can hold the box and fade to the photograph when the file is ready. The placeholder is not the photograph. It should not be so detailed that the fade feels like a glitch, and it should not be a different crop. Same frame, less information, then the real file. If you change the photograph later, change the URL. Caches are good at keeping bytes forever. A new filename, or a version in the path, is how you stop an old image from lingering under a new caption.

## Alt text that matches the frame

Alt text describes what is in the photograph. It does not describe the article's keyword, and it does not repeat the caption if the caption is right there and the alt would only duplicate it. The W3C's [WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) frames WCAG as the shared standard for web content, and informative images are part of that content. A person who does not see the image should get the information the image was carrying.

Look at the frame and write what is true. "A clothing shop with racks, rope-hung lamps, and a mirror" is alt text. "Best ecommerce photography for conversion" is a slogan stuffed into an attribute. If the image is a product, name the product and the relevant variant, color included, when color is why you showed it. If the image is atmosphere and the adjacent sentence already carries the point, you can mark it decorative and use empty alt. Decorative is a decision. Empty alt on an image that is the only explanation of a step is a missing sentence.

Write the alt when you place the image, while you can see the crop. A media library field filled in months earlier, for a different crop, will describe a subject you have since cut off. The preview of the page is the right moment to reread it. If the crop changed, the alt changes.

Captions are optional and public. They can credit the source and add a clause the alt does not need to carry. They are not a second alt. Do not hide the only copy of the information in the caption and leave the alt empty, unless the caption is programmatically associated with the figure. A `<figure>` and `<figcaption>` do that job. A gray paragraph that merely sits near the image may not.

## Weight is a design decision

A page of twelve full-bleed photographs will be heavy even if each one is well made. Choose fewer, larger moments, or accept the cost and reduce everything else: no second hero, no background video, no parallax layer of another image. The budget is the page, not the single file in isolation.

Background video is the usual way a photography page doubles its weight without a discussion. If the still frame communicates the place, use the still. If the motion is the point, the video needs a poster image that is itself cropped and light, and it needs to stay still for anyone who asked for reduced motion. The poster has to be a real frame, not a black box, because the poster is what many people will see.

Text inside photographs does not scale, does not translate, and does not meet contrast by accident. Set type in HTML over a simple area of the image, or beside it. If the type is baked in, you will ship a second image for a headline change, and the alt will have to carry the baked-in words. That is a poster, not a page.

Compression artifacts are part of the brand whether you want them or not. Look at the file at 100 percent on a cheap screen, not only on the monitor you graded it on. Blocky skies and halos around a logo in the corner are the cost of pushing quality too far down. Raise the quality or shrink the dimensions. Do not "fix" it by uploading the original and letting the browser struggle.

## A pass on one real page

Pick the page with the most photographs. Open the network panel. Reload.

- The hero is cropped to its slot and is not lazy-loaded.
- Its box is reserved, and the text does not jump when it arrives.
- A phone downloads a smaller width than a desktop.
- The format is modern, and the edges still look like the photograph.
- Alt text matches this crop, or the image is genuinely decorative.
- Changing the file means a new URL, so the cache cannot serve the old one.

If the hero is the thing pushing largest contentful paint past the 2.5 second target, reduce dimensions before you add a preloader. A preloader is a confession that the file is late. Make it less late.

Then look at the next image below the fold and confirm it can wait. Eager-loading everything "so it feels premium" spends the first view's budget on photographs the reader has not reached. Premium, on a slow phone, is the first picture arriving cleanly and the page staying still.

## The picture and the page have to agree

A photography-heavy page is often a shop, a lookbook, or a studio's own work. The images are the argument. They still have to sit in a document that loads, shifts less than 0.1 on the layout metric, and describes its frames in text. None of that asks you to use worse photographs. It asks you to decide the slot, the crop, and the words with the same care you used in the grade.

The next page, if those photographs are products, is the purchase itself. [A checkout for a shop with twenty products](/blog/a-checkout-for-a-shop-with-twenty-products) is the next piece. Twenty products do not need a marketplace checkout. They need shipping, tax, and payment on as few steps as the provider allows, with the cost visible before the last button.

If you want a set of images cut to the real slots and described honestly, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the heaviest page. The useful review starts with the hero's bytes and its crop.
